15.t: Working with data: heat and a protein’s shape
q: Calculate the percentage decrease in activity of the human enzyme between 50 and 60 °C.
Explain why the human enzyme loses activity after heating to 60 °C.
Heat breaks hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and hydrophobic interactions, so the tertiary structure changes and the active site no longer fits the substrate.
Estimate how much one extra disulfide bond raised the temperature for 50% activity. Explain the effect.

50% at about 57 °C for the human enzyme and about 65 °C with the extra bond: about 8 °C higher. A disulfide bond is covalent, so it holds two parts of the chain together and needs far more energy to break.
Suggest two features of the hot-spring enzyme that could explain its stability.
Any two: more disulfide bonds; more ionic bonds; a larger tightly packed hydrophobic core; fewer loose loops.
The enzymes were tested at 25 °C after heating. Explain why this is better than testing each at its heating temperature.
At a high test temperature, activity is affected by both faster collisions and denaturation. Testing at 25 °C shows only the permanent damage to the structure.
